comparison: Strong agreement on core modeling results (C1, C2, C3, C27, C28, C41-C43). Both find the stochastic simulation data and theoretical analysis comprehensive and sound, supporting claims about high invasiveness across parameter ranges. OpenEval notes bimodal distributions and resistance modeling; peer reviewers call it 'possibly the most comprehensive analysis to date.'

Agreement on structured population modeling (C30, C31, C47, C50, C55). Both accept the validity of containment thresholds based on migration rates. OpenEval notes simplified five-subpopulation structure as limitation; Peer Reviewer #1 raises technical questions about Figure 2E but accepts overall results. Peer Reviewer #3 explicitly endorses the structured population conclusions.

Strong disagreement on policy recommendations (C4, C5, C48, C49). OpenEval finds these logical inferences from modeling but notes they are value judgments. Peer reviewers strongly critique these claims as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer #2 stating they 'go far beyond the work presented' and appear 'arrogant.' Editor notes the 'forceful message' is not substantiated.

Complete agreement on CRISPR mechanisms and gene drive biology (C6-C16). Both treat these as well-established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. No challenges from either evaluation.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding social/ecological consequences (C44-C46). OpenEval finds these speculative without modeling evidence. Peer Reviewer #2 notes the paper 'does not actually identify any biologically serious consequence' and that drives may have 'almost no fitness consequence.' Both acknowledge social concerns but lack empirical support.

Disagreement on neutral resistance assumption (C26, C38). OpenEval finds this appropriately conservative and supports robustness claims, though notes lack of quantitative thresholds. Peer Reviewer #3 raises major concern that neutral resistance 'cannot be considered as universal' and that fitness costs 'would immediately alter the results,' marking this UNCERTAIN rather than SUPPORTED.

Partial disagreement on stochastic modeling rationale (C21, C22, C23/C58). OpenEval finds the need for stochastic modeling well-justified by established theory. Peer Reviewer #1 questions this rationale, noting Figure 9 shows deterministic and stochastic models make same predictions, asking 'why do we need stochastic models after all?' marking this UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on empirical data compilation (C18, C19). Both accept the homing efficiency ranges from published studies. OpenEval notes missing verification data and unmeasured fitness costs. Peer Reviewer #3 notes the article is 'well documented' on CRISPR systems and laboratory assays. Both find claims SUPPORTED despite data limitations.

Agreement on inbreeding analysis (C39). OpenEval supports the technical findings while noting the assumption of no inbreeding depression may be unrealistic. Peer reviewers accept Figure 9 results without challenge. Both find the technical analysis SUPPORTED.

Agreement on offspring number analysis (C52). OpenEval finds this supported by Hammond 2016 citation and appropriate scaling in Figures 5-6. Peer reviewers accept these citations and empirical data without question. Both mark as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on citation to prior work (C23). OpenEval notes appropriate contextualization of Marshall 2009. Peer reviewers accept this as straightforward citation without challenge. Both find SUPPORTED.

Overlap on deterministic theory (C58). OpenEval finds established deterministic theory supports claims. Peer Reviewer #1's questioning of stochastic modeling rationale indirectly relates to deterministic vs. stochastic approaches, but doesn't directly challenge C58 itself.

Minor overlap on 'socially tolerable threshold' (C40). OpenEval notes this concept is not quantitatively specified, making the claim somewhat subjective. Peer reviewers accept the sensitivity analyses broadly but don't specifically address the social tolerability concept in their evaluation of R1 claims.
